source.title: The Art of Money Getting
source.attribution: P. T. Barnum, The Art of Money Getting, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Avoid debt for things you will use up
cards.body:
Barnum warned young people against borrowing for food, clothes and other things that are gone long before the bill is. Paying off such debt means working for something you no longer have, which he called working for a dead horse. He made an exception for credit used to buy something that earns its own repayment.

Buy-now-pay-later, store cards and credit card balances are the modern form. They make spending feel painless today and turn future paychecks into payments for past purchases.
cards.quote: Grunting and groaning and working for what he has eaten up or worn out, and now when he is called upon to pay up, he has nothing to show for his money; this is properly termed ‘working for a dead horse.’
cards.apply_it: Check your current balances. Is any of it for something you have already eaten, worn out or forgotten? Make a plan to clear that first.

quiz.question: What kind of borrowing did Barnum see as acceptable?
options: Credit used to buy something that will turn a profit
quiz.explanation: He excepted credit used to buy something that helps repay itself, like a merchant's stock or a farmer's manure.

cards.title: Never guarantee a loan you could not afford to lose
cards.body:
Barnum's rule was blunt: do not co-sign or guarantee anyone's debt, even a parent's or sibling's, for more than you could lose without caring, unless you hold solid security. He had watched easy guarantees lead borrowers into risky side ventures and drag their friends down with them.

Co-signing a car loan, a lease or a business credit line is the modern version. If the borrower fails, the debt becomes yours. Helping family is generous; just treat any guarantee as money you may actually have to pay.
cards.quote: I hold that no man ought ever to endorse a note or become security, for any man, be it his father or brother, to a greater extent than he can afford to lose and care nothing about, without taking good security.
cards.apply_it: Before agreeing to guarantee anything, ask yourself: if I had to pay this in full tomorrow, would I be fine?

quiz.question: What was Barnum's limit on co-signing for someone without security?
options: Never more than you can afford to lose and not care about
Any amount if the person seems wealthy
quiz.explanation: He allowed it only up to an amount you could lose without it mattering, unless you took good security.

cards.title: Don't bet your savings on things you don't understand
cards.body:
Barnum saw many successful people go broke the same way. Having done well in their own line of work, they were flattered into a 'sure thing' outside it, put in more and more money as the venture demanded, and lost everything.

The pattern repeats with hot tips, hyped coins and a friend's can't-miss startup. Success in one field does not make you an expert in another. If you want to try something unfamiliar, keep the amount small enough that losing it would not hurt your life.
cards.quote: let the sums thus invested be moderate in amount, and never let a man foolishly jeopardize a fortune that he has earned in a legitimate way, by investing it in things in which he has had no experience.
cards.apply_it: List your investments. For each one, could you explain in two sentences how it makes money? Reduce anything you can't.

quiz.question: What was Barnum's advice about investing outside your own field?
options: Keep the amounts moderate and never risk your hard-earned fortune
Go all in when friends say you are lucky
quiz.explanation: He allowed modest bets on promising ventures but warned against risking a fortune on things you have no experience in.

cards.title: Do one thing at a time and finish it
cards.body:
Barnum believed that working by a simple system, with a time and place for things, prompt follow-through and punctual appointments, gets twice as much done with half the stress. The person who half-does one task, jumps to another and half-does that never knows when the day's work is finished.

He also warned against overdoing it: a system so elaborate that it becomes red tape is no better. The aim is finished work and free time, not perfect filing.
cards.quote: By introducing system into all your transactions, doing one thing at a time, always meeting appointments with punctuality, you find leisure for pastime and recreation
cards.apply_it: Pick the one task that matters most today. Close other tabs and notifications and work on it until it is done.

quiz.question: What did Barnum say a good system gives you besides more output?
quiz.explanation: Doing one thing at a time and being punctual frees up time for rest and recreation.

cards.title: The top of any field is never crowded
cards.body:
Barnum argued that no trade is overcrowded at the top. The best carpenter, doctor or merchant in town is always in demand. Most people, he said, chase quick money and do their work superficially, which leaves room for anyone who does it thoroughly and honestly.

In a crowded job market, being merely adequate means competing with everyone. Becoming clearly excellent at one thing, and reliable with it, puts you in a much smaller group that clients and employers actively seek out.
cards.quote: No profession, trade, or calling, is overcrowded in the upper story.
cards.apply_it: Name one skill central to your work. What is one deliberate step you can take this month to get noticeably better at it?

quiz.question: Why did Barnum think the best people in any trade always have enough work?
options: Because they work in big cities
Because the top of every field has room and is sought out
quiz.explanation: Few people work thoroughly, so whoever excels in their line is always in demand.

cards.title: Market a genuinely good product, and keep at it
cards.body:
Barnum, a master showman, insisted on two rules. First, only promote something that truly delivers; a poor product can sell once, but buyers will denounce you and not return. Second, do not give up after a few attempts. People need to see a message many times before they notice, read and finally act on it.

This still applies to posts, emails and ads. One launch announcement is rarely enough. Steady, honest visibility for a product people are glad they bought is what builds lasting trade.
cards.quote: So a man who advertises at all must keep it up until the public know who and what he is, and what his business is, or else the money invested in advertising is lost.
cards.apply_it: If you are promoting something, plan five honest, useful touchpoints over the next month instead of one big announcement.

quiz.question: Which pair of rules did Barnum give for advertising?
options: Rely only on word of mouth
Promote only genuine goods and keep advertising until people know you
quiz.explanation: A spurious article fails in the end, and a few insertions are wasted; you need a good product and persistence.

cards.title: Courtesy is the best capital a business can invest
cards.body:
Barnum said fine shops and flashy ads are wasted if customers are treated rudely. People return to businesses that treat them well and give fair value, and they abandon those that squeeze every deal as if they will never meet again.

In an age of online reviews, that is truer than ever. A patient support reply, a fair refund or a friendly word costs little and builds loyalty, while one dismissive interaction can travel far. Treat every customer as someone you hope to see again.
cards.quote: Politeness and civility are the best capital ever invested in business.
cards.locator: Be Polite and Kind to Your Customers ¶1
cards.apply_it: In your next interaction with a customer, client or colleague, add one small act of courtesy you would normally skip.

quiz.question: What happens, in Barnum's view, to those who drive sharp bargains as if they will never see customers again?
options: They never see those customers again
quiz.explanation: Customers treated that way do not come back, which is exactly what the sharp dealer assumed.

cards.title: Choose work that fits your natural bent
cards.body:
Barnum believed the safest start in life is choosing work that suits your own tastes and abilities. He mocked parents who hand out careers like chores, making one son a lawyer and another a watchmaker without asking what each was good at. He admitted he himself had no gift for machinery: forced into watchmaking, he would have spent his life working uphill and looking for excuses to stop.

Today's pressure may come from family, status or salary charts. Those matter, but work that runs against your grain drains effort every day. Notice what you lose track of time doing, and lean your career in that direction.
cards.quote: If a man was to take such a boy as I was, and attempt to make a watchmaker of him, the boy might, after an apprenticeship of five or seven years, be able to take apart and put together a watch; but all through life he would be working up hill
cards.apply_it: List three tasks you do without needing to be pushed. How much of your current work uses them? Pick one small way to use them more this month.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum say he would have failed as a watchmaker?
options: He had no natural liking or gift for machinery
There were too many watchmakers in town
His father refused to pay for training
quiz.explanation: Barnum said he had an aversion to machinery, so he would always be working uphill in that trade.

cards.title: A good business in the wrong place still fails
cards.body:
After the right vocation, Barnum said, comes the right location. You might run a hotel like clockwork, but put it in a village with no travellers and it will ruin you. He also warned against setting up where there are already enough people doing the same thing to meet demand.

He told of a brilliant London showman wasting his talent on a poor spot; Barnum hired him for New York, and the man later made a fortune on his own. Before opening a shop, stall or service, check who will actually pass by, and how many others already serve them.
cards.quote: It is equally important that you do not commence business where there are already enough to meet all demands in the same occupation.
cards.apply_it: Before starting a venture, count the competitors within reach and estimate how many real customers pass that spot each day.

quiz.question: According to Barnum, what can ruin a perfectly well-run hotel?
options: Being placed where no travellers come
quiz.explanation: He said a hotel run like clockwork would still fail in a village with no railroad or public travel.

cards.title: Money makes a good servant and a terrible master
cards.body:
Barnum compared money to fire. Put it to work at safe interest and it labours for you night and day, in any weather, even on Sundays. Owe it, and the same force works against you: the lender wakes up richer each morning while the borrower grows poorer in his sleep.

Compound interest is the modern name for this. A savings account, pension or sound investment quietly grows; a credit card balance or high-interest loan quietly grows too, in the wrong direction. The question for every naira, shilling or cedi is which side of the interest you are on.
cards.quote: Money is in some respects like fire; it is a very excellent servant but a terrible master.
cards.apply_it: Write down every balance that charges you interest and every account that pays you interest. Which list is growing faster?

quiz.question: What did Barnum mean by calling money a 'terrible master'?
options: Interest on debt keeps piling up against you
quiz.explanation: When you owe, interest piles up against you and keeps you down, which he called the worst kind of slavery.

cards.title: Make sure you're on the right path, then keep going
cards.body:
Barnum quoted Davy Crockett's rule: be sure you are right, then go ahead. He saw many people get close to their goal, lose faith in themselves, slacken off and miss the prize. He called the quality he admired 'go-aheaditiveness': refusing to let low moods or the blues drain your energy while you work toward independence.

The two halves matter equally. Checking first stops you charging down a bad road; persisting after that stops you quitting a good one. When motivation dips, remind yourself why you judged the path right in the first place, rather than reopening the whole decision on a bad day.
cards.quote: How many have almost reached the goal of their ambition, but, losing faith in themselves, have relaxed their energies, and the golden prize has been lost forever.
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence on why your current goal is worth it. Read it on the next day you feel like giving up.

quiz.question: What did Barnum say causes many people to lose a prize they had nearly won?
options: Bad luck at the last moment
Losing faith in themselves and easing off
quiz.explanation: He said many almost reach their goal but, losing faith in themselves, relax their energies and lose it.

cards.title: Take advice, but learn to rely on your own judgement
cards.body:
Barnum noticed that some people look on the dark side, borrow trouble, and then ask everyone for advice. They end up blown one way by one opinion and another way by the next, never committing to anything. He saw perseverance and self-reliance as two sides of the same quality.

Advice is valuable, but only if you weigh it and then decide. Collecting opinions can become a way to avoid owning a choice. Gather what you need, set a deadline, make the call yourself, and stick with it long enough to learn whether it works.
cards.quote: Until you can get so that you can rely upon yourself, you need not expect to succeed.
cards.apply_it: For a decision you keep postponing, list what you know, ask one trusted person, set a date, and decide on that date.

quiz.question: What problem did Barnum see in people who constantly ask for advice?
options: They pay too much for experts
They are governed by one wind and blown by another
quiz.explanation: He said such people cannot rely on themselves and are pushed around by each new opinion.

cards.title: Do the job thoroughly, and don't put off what can be done now
cards.body:
Barnum's advice was to work at your business with all your might, early and late if needed, leaving no stone unturned and never delaying for an hour what could be done just as well now. He pointed out that two neighbours in the same trade can end up rich and poor simply because one does the work thoroughly and the other only half does it.

Half-finished work looks like progress but rarely pays. Customers, employers and partners notice who finishes properly. Doing the full job, promptly, is one of the few advantages anyone can choose.
cards.quote: Many a man acquires a fortune by doing his business thoroughly, while his neighbor remains poor for life, because he only half does it.
cards.locator: Whatever You Do, Do It with All Your Might ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one task you have half-finished. Finish it completely today before starting anything new.

quiz.question: According to Barnum, why might one neighbour stay poor while another prospers in the same trade?
options: The poor one only half does his business
The rich one charges higher prices
quiz.explanation: Barnum said thorough work builds fortunes while half-done work keeps people poor.

cards.title: Tie your camel: do your part before trusting to luck
cards.body:
Barnum had no patience for people who wait, like Dickens's Mr. Micawber, for something to turn up. He retold a story of the Prophet Muhammad: a tired follower said he would let his camel loose and trust it to God, and the reply was to tie the camel and then trust God. Cromwell's version was to trust in Providence but keep your powder dry.

Faith, hope and good fortune are welcome, but they are not a plan. Do everything within your power first, then accept that the rest is out of your hands. That order matters.
cards.quote: Do all you can for yourselves, and then trust to Providence, or luck, or whatever you please to call it, for the rest.
cards.locator: Whatever You Do, Do It with All Your Might ¶6
cards.apply_it: Think of something you are hoping will work out. What is one concrete step you can take today to 'tie the camel'?

quiz.question: What is the lesson of 'tie thy camel, and trust it to God' as Barnum used it?
options: Do your own part first, then trust for the rest
quiz.explanation: Barnum used it to say you must do all you can yourself before leaving the rest to Providence or luck.

cards.title: Learn your business through your own hands and eyes
cards.body:
Barnum argued that no one can expect to succeed without understanding their business thoroughly, and that understanding only comes from personal application and experience. Even the best employees miss things an owner would catch, because no agent cares as much as the person whose money is at stake. Hence his line that the employer's eye is worth more than many hired hands.

Delegating is necessary, but delegating what you don't understand is risky. Whether you run a shop, a farm or a side hustle, spend time doing and checking each part yourself before handing it off.
cards.quote: The eye of the employer is often worth more than the hands of a dozen employees.
cards.locator: Depend Upon Your Own Personal Exertions ¶1
cards.apply_it: Choose one part of your work or business you have never done yourself. Spend an hour doing or closely watching it this week.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum value the owner's personal attention so highly?
options: An agent cannot be as faithful to the business as the owner
quiz.explanation: He said an agent cannot be as faithful to an employer as to himself, so owners notice what staff overlook.

cards.title: Treat each mistake as experience you've paid for
cards.body:
Barnum expected anyone running a business to make mistakes almost every day, and to learn something every day too. Mistakes, he said, are useful experience if you heed them. He liked the story of a tin-peddler who, cheated on the quality of his goods, simply said there was a little information to be gained every day and he would never be cheated that way again.

The point is to make each error buy you something. Note what happened, change the process, and move on, while keeping the stakes small enough that the lesson doesn't cost too much.
cards.quote: Thus a man buys his experience, and it is the best kind if not purchased at too dear a rate.
cards.locator: Depend Upon Your Own Personal Exertions ¶1
cards.apply_it: Write down your most recent mistake and one specific change that will stop it happening again.

quiz.question: How did the tin-peddler in Barnum's story respond to being cheated?
options: He took the seller to court
He treated it as information and resolved not to be cheated that way again
He cheated his own customers to recover
quiz.explanation: He said there was a little information to be gained every day and he would never be cheated that way again.

cards.title: Be cautious when planning and bold when acting
cards.body:
Barnum admired a maxim of the elder Rothschild: be cautious and bold. It sounds contradictory, but he explained it as care in laying plans and courage in carrying them out. Someone who is all caution never dares to act; someone who is all boldness is merely reckless and eventually fails. Speculators who win big on boldness alone, he warned, usually lose it again.

It is a useful split. Spend your caution up front: research, test, ask hard questions. Once you've decided, commit fully instead of second-guessing every step.
cards.quote: you must exercise your caution in laying your plans, but be bold in carrying them out.
cards.locator: Depend Upon Your Own Personal Exertions ¶5
cards.apply_it: For your next big decision, set aside a fixed time to question the plan. After that, act without reopening it unless facts change.

quiz.question: How did Barnum interpret the Rothschild maxim 'Be cautious and bold'?
options: Be careful in planning, bold in execution
Take risks only with other people's money
Alternate between careful and bold years
quiz.explanation: He read it as caution in laying plans and boldness in carrying them out.

cards.title: What looks like luck usually has causes behind it
cards.body:
Barnum flatly denied that luck runs anyone's life. You might find a purse of gold in the street once, but you won't find one every day, and you are as likely to lose it as to find it. Like causes produce like effects, he said: use sound methods and 'bad luck' won't stop you; fail repeatedly and there are reasons, even if you can't see them yet.

This isn't a claim that chance never matters. It's a prompt to look for causes you can change instead of blaming fortune, which leaves you nothing to work on.
cards.quote: If a man adopts the proper methods to be successful, ‘luck’ will not prevent him. If he does not succeed, there are reasons for it, although, perhaps, he may not be able to see them.
cards.locator: Depend Upon Your Own Personal Exertions ¶7
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent setback you blamed on bad luck. List two causes within your control that may also have played a part.

quiz.question: What did Barnum say about someone who keeps failing?
options: There are reasons for it, even if he can't see them
quiz.explanation: Barnum said like causes produce like effects, so repeated failure has reasons behind it.

cards.title: Hire people who think, and keep good ones with fair raises
cards.body:
Barnum called employees 'living tools' and said there is no tool you should be more particular about. Hands alone are worth little without a head; he retold Henry Ward Beecher's joke about job seekers whose fingers think, until one arrives saying he thinks all over. An experienced, thoughtful worker grows more valuable every year.

So he advised keeping such people and raising their pay reasonably over time, since replacing them throws away everything they've learned. For managers and small business owners, steady fair raises are usually cheaper than constant rehiring.
cards.quote: Those men who have brains and experience are therefore the most valuable and not to be readily parted with; it is better for them, as well as yourself, to keep them, at reasonable advances in their salaries from time to time.
cards.apply_it: If you manage anyone, identify your most thoughtful team member and check when their pay or responsibilities were last reviewed.

quiz.question: What did Barnum recommend for experienced employees who think for themselves?
options: Replace them before they ask for more
Keep them, with reasonable salary increases over time
Pay them only by the piece
Promote them out of the business
quiz.explanation: He said thoughtful, experienced workers are the most valuable and worth keeping with reasonable raises.

cards.title: Don't wait for borrowed money to start; earn your first capital
cards.body:
Barnum mocked young people who refuse to work for others while they wait for a rich relative to die or a wealthy backer to appear. He thought starting on borrowed or inherited money was one of the biggest mistakes, because money you haven't earned teaches you nothing about its value. He quoted John Jacob Astor: the first thousand dollars were harder to gather than all the millions that followed.

The effort of building your first savings is the training. Small, earned capital, handled carefully, prepares you to handle larger sums later.
cards.quote: Young men, instead of ‘waiting for dead men's shoes,’ should be up and doing
cards.apply_it: Set a modest first savings target you can reach only by your own work, and track it weekly until you hit it.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum distrust starting a business with money you haven't earned?
options: You don't yet know its value, so it is easily lost
quiz.explanation: He said money is good for nothing unless you know its value by experience; easy money tends to go easily.

cards.title: Any honest trade can be done with dignity
cards.body:
Barnum contrasted England, where the business made the man and a carpenter could not be a gentleman, with America, where the man made the business. A blacksmith, shoemaker, farmer or banker could all be respected, so long as the work was legitimate. Honest work, he added, is a double blessing: it supports the worker and serves everyone who needs what he makes.

Many people still rank jobs by status rather than usefulness. Barnum's view is a good corrective: take pride in honest work of any kind, and judge people by how they do it.
cards.quote: No matter whether he is a blacksmith, a shoemaker, a farmer, banker or lawyer, so long as his business is legitimate, he may be a gentleman.
cards.apply_it: Think of a job you've looked down on. Name two ways the people who do it make your daily life possible.

quiz.question: What did Barnum mean by saying honest business is a 'double blessing'?
options: It helps the worker and also the people he serves
It can be passed to two children
quiz.explanation: He said legitimate business helps the man engaged in it and also helps others, like the farmer feeding the tailor.

cards.title: Have a practical skill to fall back on
cards.body:
Barnum lived through booms and busts and saw people rich one day and poor the next. His advice was that every young person, son or daughter, should learn some useful trade or profession, so that if fortune turned they would have something solid to earn a living with.

The idea fits uncertain economies well. Jobs vanish, businesses fail and investments drop. A skill you can sell, whether sewing, coding, bookkeeping, plumbing or teaching, is a form of insurance no one can take from you.
cards.quote: Every man should make his son or daughter learn some useful trade or profession, so that in these days of changing fortunes of being rich today and poor tomorrow they may have something tangible to fall back upon.
cards.apply_it: If your main income stopped tomorrow, what skill could you sell? If the answer is unclear, choose one to start building this month.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum want children to learn a useful trade?
options: So they would never need to save
So they could compete with their parents
So they would have something to fall back on if fortunes changed
quiz.explanation: He saw people rich today and poor tomorrow, and wanted them to have something tangible to fall back on.

cards.title: Hope is good, but don't jump at every 'sure thing'
cards.body:
Barnum said many people stay poor because they are too visionary. Every new project looks like certain success to them, so they keep switching from one business to another, never staying long enough to make any of them work. He called it the ancient error of counting chickens before they hatch.

Optimism keeps you going, but each switch has a cost: lost time, lost money and lost learning. Before abandoning what you're doing for a shiny new idea, ask whether the new one is truly better or simply newer.
cards.quote: Every project looks to them like certain success, and therefore they keep changing from one business to another, always in hot water, always ‘under the harrow.’
cards.locator: Let Hope Predominate, but Be Not Too Visionary ¶1
cards.apply_it: Before starting any new venture, write down why your current one isn't working and what evidence shows the new one will do better.

quiz.question: What habit keeps 'too visionary' people poor, according to Barnum?
options: Constantly switching from one business to another
quiz.explanation: He said every project looks certain to them, so they keep changing businesses and are always in trouble.

cards.title: Stick to one line of work until it succeeds or clearly fails
cards.body:
Barnum advised engaging in one kind of business and sticking to it until you succeed, or until experience shows you should give it up. Constant hammering on one nail drives it home. When your attention stays on one thing, your mind keeps suggesting improvements you'd never notice with a dozen projects competing for it.

Side hustles and portfolios have their place, but spreading yourself across too many ventures often means none gets enough attention to thrive. Depth tends to beat breadth until one thing is truly working.
cards.quote: A constant hammering on one nail will generally drive it home at last, so that it can be clinched.
cards.apply_it: List every project you're currently juggling. Which one deserves most of your attention for the next three months?

quiz.question: What benefit of undivided attention did Barnum point out?
options: Your mind keeps suggesting valuable improvements
It lets you hire fewer people
quiz.explanation: He said a mind centred on one object constantly suggests improvements that would otherwise be missed.

cards.title: Grab attention creatively, then keep customers with quality
cards.body:
Barnum told how Genin, a New York hatter, paid a huge sum for the first ticket to Jenny Lind's concert, knowing the press would print his name. Millions read about 'Genin, the hatter', and people checked their own hats to see if they had one. He sold thousands of extra hats a year.

Barnum's point was that the stunt only started things: many buyers came out of curiosity, but they returned because Genin gave fair value. A clever campaign can bring someone through the door once. Only a good product brings them back.
cards.quote: This novel advertisement first struck their attention, and then, as he made a good article, they came again.
cards.apply_it: Think of one inexpensive, memorable way to get noticed. Then check: would a first-time customer want to come back?

quiz.question: Why did Genin's customers keep coming back after his famous ticket purchase?
options: Barnum ordered his staff to buy hats
He gave them good value for their money
quiz.explanation: Curiosity brought them first, but they became regulars because he gave an equivalent for their money.

cards.title: Don't win the argument and lose the customer
cards.body:
One of Barnum's ushers wanted to beat a visitor who had called him no gentleman. Barnum stopped him: thrashing the man wouldn't prove anything, and it would cost the museum a customer and his friends. If the visitor owned the place and the usher had paid to enter, resentment might make sense; but here the visitor was the one paying.

In any service job, rude customers will test you. Responding calmly isn't weakness; it protects your income and reputation. The usher, sensibly, joked that he'd like a raise for absorbing the abuse.
cards.quote: you will not convince him you are a gentleman by whipping him. I cannot afford to lose a customer.
cards.locator: Be Polite and Kind to Your Customers ¶5
cards.apply_it: Next time a customer or client is rude, pause for three breaths before answering, and ask what response protects the relationship.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum tell his usher not to fight the rude visitor?
options: The visitor was a famous man
Fighting would lose a paying customer and his friends
The usher was in the wrong
quiz.explanation: He said whipping the man would prove nothing and cost the museum a customer who would take friends elsewhere.

cards.title: The best charity helps people who are helping themselves
cards.body:
Barnum believed generosity was a duty and a pleasure, and also good sense: the liberal person attracts goodwill while the miser is avoided. But he distinguished between kinds of giving. Handing out alms without asking who needs them did little good. Quietly seeking out and helping people already struggling to improve their situation multiplied the benefit.

He also insisted that real help be practical: food for the hungry rather than a blessing in its place. Giving that combines heart and judgement does the most good.
cards.quote: The best kind of charity is to help those who are willing to help themselves.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone near you who is working hard to get ahead. What practical help could you offer them this month?

quiz.question: Which kind of giving did Barnum consider best?
options: Quietly helping those who are struggling to help themselves
Giving equally to everyone who asks
quiz.explanation: He said searching out and quietly assisting people struggling for themselves is the charity that 'scattereth and yet increaseth'.

cards.title: Keep your profits and plans to yourself
cards.body:
Barnum warned against telling neighbours how you made your money. Nothing is gained and much can be lost: you invite competition, envy and requests. He advised saying nothing about your profits, hopes, expectations or intentions, and being just as careful in letters as in conversation. If you are losing money, be especially quiet, or your reputation may suffer before you can recover.

Today that includes posts, group chats and emails. Share plans with the few people who need to know, and let results speak later.
cards.quote: Say nothing about your profits, your hopes, your expectations, your intentions.
cards.apply_it: Before posting or announcing your next plan or win, ask who actually needs to know, and whether anything is gained by telling others.

quiz.question: Why did Barnum advise special caution when your business is losing money?
options: Talking about it may cost you your reputation
quiz.explanation: He said that telling of losses could cost you your reputation.

cards.title: Honesty is the real long-term business strategy
cards.body:
Barnum called the old miser's advice, 'get money honestly if you can, but get money', both wicked and stupid. Dishonesty, he said, is the hardest way to get rich: people are found out, and once integrity is doubted nearly every door closes. Meanwhile someone known to be strictly honest, even if poor, can borrow from the whole community, because everyone knows they'll be repaid.

Trust is capital that takes years to build and moments to lose. Being reliable about money and promises opens doors that cleverness never will.
cards.quote: A man who is known to be strictly honest, may be ever so poor, but he has the purses of all the community at his disposal
cards.apply_it: List any promises or debts, however small, you haven't kept. Settle or renegotiate one this week.

quiz.question: According to Barnum, what advantage does a poor but strictly honest person have?
options: The community will lend to him because he always repays
quiz.explanation: Barnum said such a person has 'the purses of all the community at his disposal' because everyone trusts him to repay.

cards.title: Getting rich is not the same as being successful
cards.body:
For all his talk of money-getting, Barnum ended with a caution: wealth alone isn't success. There are 'rich poor men', he said, while many honest people who never had much money are richer and happier than anyone who breaks the deeper laws of good living. He saw money as good when used well, a means of widening happiness and helping others, and warned that loving it for its own sake is the root of evil.

As you chase financial goals, keep a second scorecard: your integrity, relationships and the good your money actually does.
cards.quote: To get rich, is not always equivalent to being successful. ‘There are many rich poor men,’
cards.apply_it: Write down three things besides money that would make you feel successful in five years. Are you investing in them now?

quiz.question: What did Barnum mean by 'rich poor men'?
options: People with money but without honesty or real happiness
quiz.explanation: He contrasted them with honest people of modest means who are really richer and happier.
